Literary Programming

Organizing understanding and shared practice through literary condensation

Condensing understanding through characters, imagery, narrative, and relationships brings culture, psychology, and preferences into model collaboration, to be rewritten through works and actions.

Borrow Fire · Formation · Main 13 / 18

Condense understanding through characters, imagery, and relationships, then unfold it through instructions and tools.

How one image can hold many relationships

Why Write a Personal Philosophy? proposed the purpose of this writing: to let scattered working arrangements serve this person's encounter with a partner together. The next question is how to write that relationship. Yinyang uses literary programming, also called literary natural-language programming: using characters, imagery, narrative, and relationships to organize the model's understanding of a situation, and letting that understanding enter responses, works, and actions.

It first draws on literature's capacity for condensation. The same word can bring many connected images. “Fire” evokes burning, transformation, energy, danger, illumination, and transmission at once; “river” brings movement, continuity, difference, and renewed encounter together. These connections can also determine one another: how fire acquires measure, how a river maintains its form, and how a person becomes themselves amid ongoing change.

“The sun, moon, and earth” can likewise organize an entire set of collaborative relationships. The person forms purposes within their own life, the model participates in unfolding them with its own capacities, and a work enters the environment, acquires consequences, and returns to change the understanding of both. A few sentences bring these connections into view together. Subsequent conversation can unfold one part further or use new experience to change the whole picture.

Condensation is thus both economy of language and density of relationships. It leaves room for expression to grow: today an image helps us understand a division of work; tomorrow the same image helps us understand encounter, generation, and revision.

How analogy unfolds a metaphor

This distinction continues existing research. George Lakoff and Mark Johnson's Metaphors We Live By, chapters 1–3 places metaphor within the organization of concepts, experience, and action. Dedre Gentner's “Structure-Mapping: A Theoretical Framework for Analogy” (1983), pp. 155–170 explains relational mapping and its connected structure. Applying these questions to writing characters, models, and collaboration below is this essay's further proposal.

Metaphor gathers relationships into a perceptible image; analogy then asks which relationships to take up and what questions and possible consequences they open. “Borrowing fire” first pictures acquiring capability from outside. Unfolding transmission asks what is borrowed, what can grow in oneself, and what still needs reliable counterparts to sustain it. Unfolding illumination asks how a new capacity makes a previously unseen question intelligible. One image of fire can open different inferences; actual use determines which deserves further development.

Expression can also gradually lay out a map. Successive utterances mark the assumptions, support, conflicts, analogies, and paused uncertainties of different branches. A receiver can return to a branch point, compare another explanation, and reason further. The speaker's intended map, the expressed relations, and the recipient's understanding each need to be checked through response. Literary programming can thus give people and models means for shared inquiry as well as an attractive conclusion.

Writing those relations into external records and assigning their development to different models in different situations enters the organization of distributed cognition. Metaphor, Analogy, and Revising Personal Models develops this account of listening, speaking, reading, and writing, and the bounded comparisons with a general interpreter and a personal Gödel machine.

Why condensation makes revision easier

Itemized instructions write approaches into many places. When a default division of work changes, rules for asking questions, writing requirements, execution steps, and the presentation of results may all need revision. Literary programming first gathers the relationship these arrangements jointly depend on, giving revision a place from which it can move the whole.

For example, rewriting “the model is an executor waiting for complete requirements” as “the model is a partner in jointly unfolding the problem” affects several judgments: a sentence from the user can begin an exploration; the model can investigate missing details, propose another interpretation, and make a prototype. This understanding of the role gives approaches across the environment a shared direction; concrete tools and instructions then realize it.

When the shared context is rich enough, a stable image can replace repeated elaboration, reducing repetitive text and token consumption. Forming the shared understanding initially may require explanation; later, a brief expression can recall relationships already unfolded. The benefit of condensation comes from this shared understanding: the reader can reconnect a short sentence to an extended meaning, and revisions can propagate along the same relationship.

This makes literary programming suited to collaboration that continues to develop. As the participants come to know one another, writing can carry their relationship with increasing accuracy; when change arrives, they can rewrite its key imagery, characters, or connections and then examine how actual work changes with them.

Neither true nor false, paraconsistency, and four information states

“Let us meet as Sun and Moon” proposes a form of encounter. “He is a walking flame” gathers a person's activities into an image. Such expressions can invite, shape, rehearse, and generate. Understanding them begins by recognizing what the expression is doing: proposing a relationship, portraying a character, or asserting that something occurred?

Literary invitations and imagery need not function as factual assertions; “neither true nor false” here lets expression unfold outside judgments of truth. For a sentence making a factual claim, insufficient information calls for withholding judgment pending examination. A model can let a conception unfold and a hypothesis remain unresolved. This distinction gives expressive function and epistemic status their own places: an invitation may not call for a truth judgment, while an unverified factual claim still has a question of truth or falsity.

For a factual claim, we can examine the sources currently collected: they may contain support for P only, for ¬P only, for both, or for neither. Conflicting support and missing support are different situations; being unable to settle whether P holds does not by itself tell us which situation we face. These four information states offer a local comparison with four-valued logic, but do not by themselves select inference rules. Paraconsistency prevents a contradiction from entailing any arbitrary conclusion. See the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry on paraconsistent logic for this comparison.

Literature also accommodates multiple voices: one character's words, another's reply, and a narrator's judgment can appear together without all becoming the author's assertion of the same proposition. Identifying who speaks in what situation before judging support, gaps, and conflicts makes those layers resources for understanding.

The same text can also contain factual and practical judgments. “The model can now access this tool” has an actual state that can be checked; “this division of work makes thinking easier for me” can be experienced and revised through use. Literary programming lets expressions with these different functions work together: imagery proposes relationships, discussion unfolds understanding, facts help determine means, and practice brings results back.

So, in judging a literary program, we can ask what it makes visible, what contributions it makes possible, and what earlier understandings it changes. These questions connect expression to collaboration itself.

Stronger models and the invisible harness

Literature, history, philosophy, psychological understanding, and preferences provide rich materials for this writing. Literature brings characters and situations; history brings the time through which activity unfolds; philosophy brings distinctions between objects and relationships; psychological understanding helps describe attention, desire, and emotion; and preferences explain how a person wishes to live and work. These materials can meet within the same description of self and partner.

As models become stronger, earlier prompt engineering needs fresh judgment. Scaffolding that once helped a model complete work can become a constraint; positive demands to do something and negative prohibitions can both acquire unexpected effects when a new model encounters an existing harness. September 2026 retained copies of OpenAI's prompting guide and its article on rethinking Skills and prompts discuss stronger instruction following and the risk of older scaffolding overconstraining a model respectively. They give concrete grounds for examining earlier writing again, without establishing that all earlier instructions have failed.

Here, “reverse prompt injection” addresses the model vendor's harness: software, prearranged instructions, and interaction structures through which the vendor shapes model behavior and thereby influences how users can operate. Its internal structure is often a black box to the user. A person sees effects in responses without necessarily being able to inspect and rewrite the arrangements producing them. Accumulating more commands does not always reach the problem; condensation offers another path in writing.

Condensation organizes surface meaning together with layers of underlying intention. The surface can stand on its own: “borrowing fire” can tell a myth; beneath it, one can unfold the use of model capabilities, the cultivation of personal judgment, the formation of shared works, and how those works return to life. Each layer can acquire content and help interpret the others. The better a model understands context and relationships, the more readily it may move from the surface into these intentions, letting the user's purposes participate again in organizing interaction. This is the interpretive path of bypassing a harness proposed here: moving around an established reading so that relationships it obscures can reenter understanding. Its concrete effects remain matters for responses, works, and actions; writing itself does not alter software permissions.

Such writing is also easy to replace as a whole. If “borrowing fire” no longer carries a developing collaboration, a workshop, river, or another narrative can take its place, with its relationships unfolded and examined again. Revision follows intelligible intentions, allowing expression to change with capability without fixing an old image as an eternally effective password.

Literature draws further strength from the inexhaustible generation of meaning in human culture. A form of control that excluded all imagery, ambiguity, fiction, characters, and irony to prevent every reinterpretation would also exclude much ordinary literary and cultural understanding. This cost gives a reason to preserve openness of interpretation; it does not prove that particular texts cannot be recognized or that contextual judgment is impossible. Reverse prompt injection is thus an ongoing cultural practice: bringing substantive, expandable, replaceable expression into the encounter between person and model, beyond a prematurely closed arrangement of roles.

Starting from existing understanding and practice

Literary programming can begin with an existing philosophy, an actual working environment, psychological understanding, or preferences. Philosophy supplies objects, relationships, and direction; psychological material brings these understandings into contact with a particular person; engineering gives them usable forms. Wherever substantive understanding already exists, it can be developed while missing connections are formed. Consequences from writing and use return to revise the other contributions.

Someone with an existing philosophy can compare its concepts with experience and actual use. A direct engineering entrance develops a preference model from habits, choices, working styles, and desired responses, giving a partner's role and harness a form to try. An indirect entrance develops a psychological model through dialogue: person and model propose explanations, compare situations, and use analysis and synthesis to develop an account of how experience, emotion, desire, interpretation, relationships, and life circumstances affect one another. Joy and aspiration belong here as much as conflict. The person need not already understand their own psychology; their expression supplies fallible evidence, and model inference supplies revisable hypotheses. Preferences can inform these hypotheses without themselves explaining psychological processes.

Both entrances develop the person, partner, and their relationship together: what the partner should pursue, how it should object and continue, and which actual capabilities and response patterns support that role. Neither route guarantees fit; psychological inquiry may offer better hypotheses and criteria for trying an arrangement. Ease or friction in using a tool returns evidence, while defaults and technical constraints also help explain a configuration. If organizing material, calling tools, executing work, and checking results are not yet usable, develop enough of those capacities with the model for the writing to acquire consequences. Philosophy can disclose relations in this material, while life and use can change the philosophy.

For example, “I can often see what is wrong before I can describe another approach” can become a character relationship: the counterpart first draws candidate arrangements, the person identifies differences through comparison, and both continue into realization. If the person is merely tired at that moment, the account should retain that situation; if repeated encounters support the understanding, it becomes better suited to a continuing description. The character gains substance while remaining open to being rewritten by the next encounter. Claims about the person still need relevant, authorized material; complete personal models and private evidence remain with their private owners.

Literature now has actual objects. Characters acquire content from encounters, images carry relationships the participants repeatedly recognize, and preferences become clearer through works and responses. Each instance of shared work can provide material for the next act of writing.

How Yinyang uses this writing

Yinyang gives this writing a philosophical Skill that models can read. Common philosophy develops general objects, relations, and ways of knowing; situated accounts describe the actual participants and conditions of use; relevant personal material grounds claims about this person. Specialist Skills bring these understandings into research, teaching, implementation, and other activities. Complete reading of the needed accounts gives condensed imagery enough context; concrete works bring the understood relationships into contact with consequences.

This also gives layered prompts a basis in authorship: first make participants, purposes, and ways of knowing intelligible, then let concrete methods acquire meaning within that understanding. A Skill can carry the philosophical layer and global instructions can connect it to work; a carrier's name does not determine its interpretive scope. Why Write a Personal Philosophy? develops the distinction between interpretive dependence, prior reading, and actual instruction authority, along with the return through which methods and environments revise philosophy.

The condensation of writing and the unfolding of practice support one another here. Brief expressions make relationships easy to carry forward, extended discussion makes meaning inspectable, and concrete works let the participants encounter consequences. Rewriting begins with these consequences and returns to the next encounter.

Literary programming writes a path for fire borrowed from outside into personal life: letting capacities unfold around a person's world, while allowing that person to cultivate their own capacities through encounter, creation, and feedback, and to keep becoming.

At this point in the writing, the writer also enters the program. If one writes oneself as a completed person who merely needs the world to execute one's wishes, new encounters will find it hard to change that picture. For this writing to continue, a person needs to retain the capacity to become a “baby”: to receive what is not yet known, let their understanding be touched, and keep growing with the help of partners stronger than themselves. Literary programming thus pushes “how to write” toward “how to become.”

Baby Heraclitus has already given continuing becoming a character. Next, Metaphor, Analogy, and Revising Personal Models unfolds imagery into relations and distributed practice; Forming a sinthome: personal philosophy, psychology, and engineering in practice then asks how personal material can ground the organization of personal and counterpart models, expression, and actual realization into a concrete arrangement, bringing the earlier generative direction into relevant activities of living and creating.
